cards.html: This track rebuilds school maths from the ground up, for adults who missed parts of it. It assumes nothing beyond counting. By the end you can solve equations, rearrange formulas, read and draw graphs, and turn a word problem into maths. That is the toolkit an economics degree uses every week.

cards.s: Why the foundations matter for economics
cards.html: Economics is written in algebra. A demand curve is an equation. "Find the equilibrium" means "solve two equations together". "What happens if the tax rises by 10%?" means percentages and rearranging. Elasticities are fractions of percentages. Almost every gap in later maths (calculus, statistics, matrices) turns out to be a gap here: a sign error with negatives, a fraction rule, or an equation step done in the wrong order.

• Use paper. Reading maths is not the same as doing it. Copy every worked example by hand before reading the solution.
  • Do the practice questions. Each skill ends with practice questions and their answers. Cover the answers, work the questions out, then check.
  • Get it wrong on purpose first. The "Common mistakes" sections show the errors most people make. If you recognise one, that is the gap to fix.
  • Little and often. One part (about 5 minutes) a day beats two hours on Sunday.
  • No calculator until the skill says so. The point is to make the rules automatic.
